evidence.description: The class uses a shared singleton instance 'shared' while also having a public initializer.

candidates.explanation: Providing a public initializer alongside a shared singleton instance allows for multiple instances of the class to be created, which can lead to inconsistent state if the class is intended to be a singleton.
candidates.title: Public Initializer with Singleton

evidence.description: ISO8601DateFormatter is instantiated inside the lastUpdatedDate method.

candidates.explanation: Instantiating DateFormatter inside a frequently called method is inefficient. DateFormatters are expensive to create and should be reused or stored in a static property.
candidates.title: Expensive Object Creation in Method

evidence.description: The loop manually switches on statistic names and updates properties individually.

candidates.explanation: The logic for updating properties based on names is hardcoded and repetitive. This creates a maintenance burden where adding a new statistic requires updating multiple locations (the enum, the property declarations, and the switch statement).
candidates.title: Repetitive Mapping Logic

evidence.description: The URLSession data(from:) call ignores the response object.

candidates.explanation: Ignoring the URLResponse object prevents the code from checking for HTTP status codes or other response metadata, which can lead to attempting to decode error bodies as valid statistics.
candidates.title: Ignored Response Object

evidence.description: Multiple properties are declared as public internal(set).

candidates.explanation: The use of 'public internal(set)' is a contradiction in access levels. Properties should either be public with public setters or internal with internal setters. In Swift, 'public internal(set)' is not a standard access modifier; it likely indicates a misunderstanding of access levels or a typo in the modifier usage.
candidates.title: Conflicting Access Modifiers
